name: Soylent meal replacement diet

card.summary: A powdered or bottled nutritionally complete drink that some people use to replace regular meals, making calorie intake easy to measure and control for a leaner physique.
card.note: Complete-meal replacement drinks have had ingredient recalls and heavy-metal labelling disputes; exclusive use is a dietary choice with a long-term research gap.

quick.overview:
Soylent is a brand of meal-replacement drink created by software engineer Rob Rhinehart in 2013, sold as powder to mix with water or as ready-to-drink bottles. It is formulated to supply protein, fats, carbohydrates, vitamins and minerals in set amounts per serving.

For people working on their looks, the appeal is practical: a fixed-calorie drink makes it simple to run a planned deficit or maintain a steady intake, which supports fat loss and a leaner face and body. Published research on the product itself is small and mostly clinical.
quick.how: People replace one or more meals per day with a prepared serving, mixing powder with water or drinking a bottle, and often keep ordinary meals for the rest of the day. Some users in diet and lifting communities treat it as a way to hit a calorie or protein target on busy days. Because each serving has a stated calorie count, users track intake by counting servings.
quick.risks: Reviewers and users have reported digestive effects such as gas and nausea, and in 2016 the company paused sales of its powder and bar after complaints of gastrointestinal illness. A 2015 California Proposition 65 notice concerned lead and cadmium labelling, with the company saying its product was safe. Exclusive long-term use has not been studied in healthy people; people with medical conditions or allergies to soy or other ingredients are advised to check ingredients.

lead: Soylent is a commercial meal-replacement drink that began as a homemade formula. Software engineer Rob Rhinehart bought about 35 ingredients in January 2013 and refined a drink designed to meet nutritional needs without conventional cooking; he co-founded Soylent Nutrition with three other engineers and raised roughly $1.5 million in crowdfunded preorders.[1] The name comes from the food in Harry Harrison's 1966 novel Make Room! Make Room!, which Rhinehart said he chose for its provocative associations.[1]

In looksmaxxing and fitness circles the drink is discussed as a diet tool. Fixed-composition servings let a person set calories and protein precisely, which is the foundation of planned fat loss or lean bulking, and the leaner physique or sharper facial definition that follows is the appearance payoff.

Research on the product is limited. One phase II study used Soylent as an exclusive liquid nutrition source for head and neck cancer patients undergoing chemoradiation, and a small randomised trial looked at gut microbiome changes during a short Soylent diet.[2][3][4]

chain: Replace a meal with a measured-calorie serving
Steadier deficit or maintenance, leaner physique
angle.text: Because every serving has a stated calorie and macronutrient content, users treat it as a way to control intake without cooking or weighing food. Fat loss from a sustained deficit is what shows up in the face and body.

paras: Soylent is sold in powdered form and as ready-to-drink shakes. A bar was also sold until 2016.[1] The original formula included ingredients such as maltodextrin, olive oil, potassium gluconate and calcium carbonate; later versions added soy-based and algal ingredients, flavourings and sweeteners.[1] Rhinehart said his homemade version cut his monthly food spending from about $470 to $155.[1]

Soylent Nutrition began shipping in April 2014. It raised $20 million in January 2015 in a round led by Andreessen Horowitz and $50 million in 2017 led by GV; Rhinehart stepped down as chief executive in 2017.[1] Starco Brands acquired the company in 2023.[1]

In August 2015 the advocacy group As You Sow filed a Proposition 65 notice, arguing the product lacked warnings for lead and cadmium. The levels were below federal limits but above California's labelling thresholds, and the company called the product completely safe.[1] In October 2016 Soylent halted sales of its bar after reports of nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, later pausing powder sales and attributing the problem to algal flour.[1] Reviewers in major outlets gave mixed assessments of taste and experience, and several reported gastrointestinal effects.[1]
Hacker News carried extended discussion of a 2016 episode in which a company executive faced possible criminal charges over an experiment at a Los Angeles hilltop property.[5]

Soylent appears in looks-forum diet threads, usually as a convenient bulk or cut aid or as cultural shorthand, and community posts mention it alongside whole-food diets rather than as a formal protocol.

A phase II single-institution study placed head and neck cancer patients who reached 5 percent body weight loss during chemoradiation onto Soylent for all nutrition and measured quality of life and adherence.[2][3] A randomised trial posted as a preprint reported that a short interventional Soylent diet raised the Bacteroidetes to Firmicutes ratio in 14 participants' gut microbiome.[4] No published trial has tested Soylent for fat loss or appearance outcomes in healthy adults.

timeline.event: Rob Rhinehart builds the first formula; crowdfunding raises about $1.5 million.[1]
$20 million funding round; Proposition 65 notice filed.[1]
Bar and powder sales paused after gastrointestinal complaints.[1]
